label: PYQ-style
stem: What is biopiracy? Give one example involving India.
hint: Basmati, 1997.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 3 lines · 3 minutes*

**Biopiracy** is the <mark>use of bio-resources (and traditional knowledge) by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned, and without compensatory payment</mark>.

**Example:** in <u>1997</u> an American company got patent rights on <mark>Basmati rice</mark> through the US Patent and Trademark Office, although the variety was derived from Indian farmers' varieties. Attempts were also made to patent uses and products of <u>turmeric</u> and <u>neem</u>.

- one Indian example (<u>Basmati</u>, turmeric or neem)

label: PYQ-style
stem: Explain how RNA interference has been used to make tobacco plants resistant to the nematode Meloidogyne incognita.
hint: Agrobacterium, sense and anti-sense RNA.
model_answer: *How much to write: 6–7 lines (a flow sketch helps) · 5 minutes* - The nematode *Meloidogyne incognita* infects the roots of tobacco and causes a great reduction in yield. - **RNA interference (RNAi)** takes place in all eukaryotes as a cellular defence: a specific mRNA is silenced by a complementary dsRNA molecule that binds to it and prevents its translation. - Using *Agrobacterium* vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into the host plant. - The introduced DNA produced both sense and anti-sense RNA in the host cells; being complementary, they formed dsRNA, which initiated RNAi. - The dsRNA silenced the specific mRNA of the nematode, so the parasite could not survive in the transgenic host, which was protected. :::tip Your answer must contain - RNAi = dsRNA silences a specific mRNA - genes introduced with *Agrobacterium* - sense + anti-sense RNA → dsRNA - nematode mRNA silenced → parasite cannot survive ::: **Marks are lost for:** saying the plant's own mRNA is silenced; leaving out the vector; saying the toxin kills the nematode.

scheme.step: Nematode infects roots; RNAi = dsRNA silencing mRNA
Agrobacterium introduces nematode genes; sense + anti-sense → dsRNA
Nematode mRNA silenced; parasite dies; plant protected

label: PYQ-style
stem: *A four-year-old child has repeated serious infections. Tests show that a gene for an enzyme essential to the immune system has been deleted. Doctors consider three options: bone marrow transplant, injecting the missing enzyme, and gene therapy.*

parts.stem: Name the enzyme deficiency and the year of the first clinical gene therapy for it.

scheme.step: ADA deficiency; 1990

parts.stem: What is injecting the missing enzyme called, and why is it not a complete cure?
parts.model_answer: Enzyme replacement therapy; the enzyme is used up and the gene defect remains, so treatment must be repeated.

scheme.step: Enzyme replacement therapy; not curative, repeated

parts.stem: Describe the gene therapy procedure and explain why repeated treatment is needed.
parts.model_answer: Lymphocytes from the child's blood are grown in culture; a functional ADA cDNA is introduced using a retroviral vector; the cells are returned to the child. The engineered lymphocytes are not immortal, so periodic infusions are needed; introducing the gene at an early embryonic stage could give a permanent cure.

scheme.step: Lymphocytes cultured, ADA cDNA via retroviral vector, reinfused
Cells not immortal → periodic infusions

hint: The enzyme is adenosine deaminase. Injected enzyme gets used up; engineered lymphocytes do not live for ever.
model_answer:
*How much to write: one line each for (i) and (ii), 3–4 lines for (iii) · 6 minutes*

**(i)** <mark>Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency</mark>; the first clinical gene therapy was given in <mark>1990</mark> to a 4-year-old girl.

**(ii)** <u>Enzyme replacement therapy</u>: functional ADA is given by injection. It is not a complete cure because the <mark>gene defect remains</mark>, so the treatment must be repeated.

**(iii)** <u>Lymphocytes</u> from the patient's blood are grown in culture outside the body. A functional <mark>ADA cDNA is introduced into them using a retroviral vector</mark>, and the cells are returned to the patient. As these cells are <mark>not immortal</mark>, the patient needs periodic infusions of genetically engineered lymphocytes. If the gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA were introduced into cells at an <u>early embryonic stage</u>, it could be a permanent cure.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- (i) <mark>ADA</mark>, <mark>1990</mark>
- (ii) enzyme replacement; gene defect remains
- (iii) lymphocytes + <u>ADA cDNA via retroviral vector</u>; cells mortal → periodic infusions
:::

**Marks are lost for:** giving 1983 as the year; saying the gene is put into red blood cells.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
(a) Why was insulin from cattle and pigs replaced? Describe how human insulin was produced by recombinant DNA technology. [3]
(b) Give two uses of transgenic animals with an example each. [2]
hint: Allergy; chains A and B.
model_answer: *How much to write: about two-thirds of a page with a small sketch · 9 minutes* **(a)** Insulin taken from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs caused some patients to develop allergy or other reactions to the foreign protein. Insulin has two short polypeptide chains, A and B, linked by disulphide bridges. In the body it is made as a pro-hormone, pro-insulin, with an extra stretch, the C peptide, which is removed during maturation. In 1983, Eli Lilly prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to the A and B chains, introduced them into plasmids of *E. coli* to produce the chains separately, then extracted the chains and combined them by creating disulphide bonds to form human insulin. **(b)** Any two uses, with examples: - **Biological products:** α-1-antitrypsin (to treat emphysema); Rosie, the first transgenic cow (1997), gave milk with human α-lactalbumin. - **Study of disease:** transgenic models for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Alzheimer's. - **Vaccine safety:** transgenic mice used to test the safety of the polio vaccine. - **Chemical safety testing:** toxicity testing with animals more sensitive to toxic substances. - **Normal physiology:** e.g. study of insulin-like growth factor. :::tip Your answer must contain - allergy to animal insulin - A + B chains, disulphide bridges, pro-insulin with C peptide - Eli Lilly 1983: chains made separately in *E. coli*, then joined - two uses, each with an example ::: **Marks are lost for:** saying the whole pro-insulin was expressed; giving uses without examples.

scheme.step: Allergy from animal insulin
Structure: A and B chains, disulphide bonds, pro-insulin with C peptide
Eli Lilly: A and B genes in E. coli plasmids, chains joined
Two uses with examples (1 each)

label: PYQ-style
stem: Why are molecular methods needed for early diagnosis of disease? Explain how PCR, a radioactive probe and ELISA are used in molecular diagnosis.
hint: Conventional tests need the pathogen in large numbers or symptoms to appear.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 7–8 lines · 5 minutes*

Early diagnosis allows effective treatment, but <u>conventional methods</u> (serum and urine analysis) cannot detect a disease until the <mark>pathogen concentration is high or symptoms have appeared</mark>.

- **PCR:** amplifies even a very small amount of pathogen nucleic acid, so it detects <u>HIV in suspected AIDS patients</u> early and finds <u>mutations in genes of suspected cancer patients</u>.
- **Probe and autoradiography:** a <u>single-stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule</u> is allowed to hybridise with its complementary DNA in a clone of cells. A clone with a <mark>mutated gene does not appear on the photographic film</mark>, because the probe cannot pair with it.
- **ELISA:** based on the principle of <mark>antigen–antibody interaction</mark>; it detects the pathogen's antigens (proteins, glycoproteins) or the antibodies made against the pathogen.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- why conventional methods fail early
- PCR detects <u>HIV</u> and cancer mutations
- labelled <u>probe</u>: mutated gene does not show
- ELISA = <mark>antigen–antibody interaction</mark>
:::

**Marks are lost for:** saying ELISA amplifies DNA; reversing which clone shows on the film.

scheme.step: Need for early detection; PCR use
Radioactive probe with autoradiography
ELISA principle and use

label: PYQ-style
stem: What is gene therapy? Describe the first clinical gene therapy, given in 1990, and explain why it does not give a permanent cure.
hint: A four-year-old girl, the enzyme adenosine deaminase, lymphocytes and a retroviral vector.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 6–8 lines · 5 minutes*

**Gene therapy** is a collection of methods that allow <mark>correction of a gene defect diagnosed in a child or embryo</mark>: genes are inserted into the person's cells to treat a hereditary disease, compensating for a non-functional gene.

**First clinical gene therapy (1990):** given to a <u>4-year-old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency</u>; the ADA enzyme is crucial for the immune system, and the disorder is caused by deletion of its gene.
1. <u>Lymphocytes</u> from the patient's blood were grown in culture.
2. A functional <mark>ADA cDNA</mark> was introduced into them using a <u>retroviral vector</u>.
3. The lymphocytes were returned to the patient.

**Not permanent:** these cells are <mark>not immortal</mark>, so the patient needs periodic infusions of genetically engineered lymphocytes. A permanent cure could come if the ADA gene from marrow cells were introduced into cells at an <u>early embryonic stage</u>.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- definition of gene therapy
- <u>ADA deficiency</u>, lymphocytes, <mark>ADA cDNA via retroviral vector</mark>
- cells mortal → <u>periodic infusions</u>; early-embryo route for permanent cure
:::

**Marks are lost for:** saying the gene was put into red blood cells; missing the retroviral vector.

scheme.step: Definition of gene therapy
ADA deficiency; lymphocytes + functional ADA cDNA by retroviral vector
Not permanent: periodic infusion; early embryonic stage

label: PYQ-style
stem:
(a) How has the gene from *Bacillus thuringiensis* been used to make cotton resistant to insects? Explain why the Bt toxin does not kill the bacterium but kills the insect. [3]
(b) Why has the Indian Government set up GEAC? State one ethical concern about genetically modified organisms. [2]
hint: (a) cry genes; inactive protoxin, alkaline gut, pores in the midgut. (b) Safety of releasing GM organisms.
model_answer:
*How much to write: about two-thirds of a page · 9 minutes*

**(a)** *Bacillus thuringiensis* forms protein crystals containing a toxic <u>insecticidal protein</u>.
- In the bacterium the toxin exists as an <mark>inactive protoxin</mark>, so the bacterium is not harmed.
- When an insect larva eats it, the <mark>alkaline pH of the insect gut</mark> solubilises the crystals and converts the protoxin into the <u>active toxin</u>.
- The active toxin <u>binds the surface of midgut epithelial cells</u> and creates pores; the cells swell and lyse, and the insect dies.
- The toxin is coded by <u>cry genes</u>: <mark>cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms</mark>; cryIAb controls corn borer. These genes were introduced into cotton to make **Bt cotton**, which makes its own toxin, so less pesticide is needed.

**(b)** **GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee)** <mark>makes decisions on the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services</mark>.
Ethical concern (any one): GM organisms released into ecosystems may have unpredictable effects; using animals for producing proteins may cause them suffering; companies patenting products based on traditional knowledge (<u>biopiracy</u>, e.g. Basmati rice) without compensation.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- <mark>inactive protoxin</mark> in the bacterium
- <mark>alkaline gut pH</mark> activates; pores in <u>midgut</u> cells, lysis
- <u>cryIAc, cryIIAb</u> for bollworms
- GEAC: validity of GM research + safety of release; one ethical issue
:::

**Marks are lost for:** saying the toxin is activated by acid; naming cryIAb for cotton bollworms; describing GEAC as a patent office.

scheme.step: Inactive protoxin in bacterium; alkaline gut activates it
Binds midgut cells, pores, lysis
cry genes named; transferred to cotton
Role of GEAC
One ethical concern

label: PYQ-style
stem: Insulin is made in the body as a pro-hormone. How does it mature, and how did Eli Lilly avoid this step when producing human insulin by rDNA technology?
hint: There is an extra C peptide.
model_answer: *How much to write: 3–4 lines + a small sketch · 4 minutes* Insulin is made as pro-insulin, which has an extra stretch, the C peptide. During maturation the C peptide is removed, leaving the A and B chains held together by disulphide bridges. **Eli Lilly (1983)** prepared two DNA sequences for the A and B chains, introduced them into plasmids of *E. coli* to make the chains separately, then extracted and joined them by disulphide bonds, so no C peptide had to be removed. :::tip Your answer must contain - pro-insulin, C peptide removed, A + B joined by disulphide bonds - A and B chains made separately in *E. coli* and combined ::: **Marks are lost for:** saying the whole pro-insulin gene was expressed; leaving out disulphide bonds.

scheme.step: Pro-insulin; C peptide removed; A + B with disulphide bridges
A and B chains made separately in E. coli, then joined

label: PYQ (2025)
stem: (a) Why are transgenic animals so called? (b) With one example each, explain the role of transgenic animals in (i) vaccine safety and (ii) biological products.
hint: Polio vaccine and mice; Rosie the cow.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 6–7 lines · 5 minutes*

**(a)** Their DNA has been manipulated to <mark>possess and express an extra (foreign) gene</mark>.

**(b)(i) Vaccine safety:** <u>transgenic mice</u> are being developed to test the safety of vaccines before they are used on humans, e.g. the <mark>polio vaccine</mark>; if reliable they could replace monkeys.

**(ii) Biological products:** transgenic animals carry the gene for a useful product. Example: human protein <u>α-1-antitrypsin</u> to treat emphysema; <mark>Rosie</mark>, the first transgenic cow (1997), gave milk with <u>human alpha-lactalbumin</u> (2.4 g per litre).

:::tip Your answer must contain

- transgenic mice: <mark>polio vaccine</mark> safety
- α-1-antitrypsin or Rosie's <u>alpha-lactalbumin</u>
:::

**Marks are lost for:** writing beta-lactalbumin; giving Bt cotton (a plant) as an example.

label: PYQ (2025)
stem: (a) Mention two advantages of micropropagation. (b) Briefly describe how it is done in the laboratory. (c) Name two food plants grown commercially by this method.
hint: Explant, nutrient medium, somaclones.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 6 lines · 4 minutes · not in boards 2026–27*

**(a)** <mark>Thousands of plants in a very short time</mark>; all are <u>genetically identical</u> to the parent (somaclones).

**(b)** A small piece of plant, the <u>explant</u>, is grown under <u>sterile conditions</u> on a nutrient medium with a carbon source (sucrose), inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids and growth regulators (auxins, cytokinins). It regenerates whole plants (<mark>totipotency</mark>), which are then moved to soil.

**(c)** <u>Tomato, banana, apple</u> (any two).

:::tip Your answer must contain
- large numbers quickly; <u>somaclones</u>
- explant + sterile nutrient medium + growth regulators
- two of tomato, banana, apple
:::

**Marks are lost for:** confusing micropropagation with somatic hybridisation.

scheme.step: Two advantages
Explant on sterile nutrient medium regenerates whole plants
Two food plants (tomato, banana, apple)
